note: Text rules. Every rule applies in every mode, creative included, by the owner's decision. Hard rules gate; advisory rules are reported for judgment. mikedesign loads this file to check the words on rendered pages.

rules.title: Fabricated testimonial or attribution
rules.why: Invented people presented as real customers. Beyond being a tell, it is a claim you cannot stand behind.
rules.fix: Use a real quote with a real name, or cut the section until you have one.

rules.title: Round invented metric presented as fact
rules.why: '10,000+ happy customers' and '99.9% uptime' with nothing behind them. An invented number reads as a real claim.
rules.fix: Use a measured number, or make the point without one.

rules.title: Em dash in interface copy
rules.why: One of the most reliable machine-written markers, and against house style.
rules.fix: Restructure with commas, colons, parentheses, or two sentences.

rules.title: Filler phrasing that carries no information
rules.why: Sentences shaped like value propositions that say nothing specific about this product.
rules.fix: Say the concrete thing the product does, in the product's own language.

rules.title: Rule-of-three phrasing
rules.why: 'Faster, simpler, and smarter.' A rhythm models reach for when there is nothing specific to say. Rendered text is matched anywhere, because the role is already known. Source text is matched only inside a heading, because a mid-paragraph list of three real things is not this tell.
rules.fix: Keep the one claim that is true and specific. Cut the two that pad the rhythm.

rules.title: Raw model output left in the copy
rules.why: Citation stubs and assistant disclaimers that exist only because text was pasted straight out of a chat window. Nothing else explains them being there.
rules.fix: Delete them. Where a citation was actually meant, write the real link.

test.pattern: (contentReference|oaicite|turn\d+search\d+|\[cite:\s*\d+\]|\[span_\d+\]|grok_render|ppl-ai-file-upload|as an AI language model|my (knowledge|training) (cut-?off|data)|I do not have access to real-?time)

rules.title: Not just X, it is Y
rules.why: The most recognizable sentence shape in machine-written copy. It promises a distinction, then supplies both halves itself, so the reader learns nothing they were not handed.
rules.fix: Keep the half that is true and specific. The setup was never carrying information.

test.pattern: \b(not just|isn'?t just|is not just|not only|no longer just)\b[^.!?]{0,60}?\b(but|it'?s|they'?re|its)\b

rules.title: Opening that delays the claim
rules.why: 'In today's fast-paced world' and its relatives occupy the space where the first real sentence should be.
rules.fix: Delete the opener, start at the claim, and check whether anything died.

test.pattern: \b(in (today'?s|an era of|a world (of|where))\s|let'?s (dive in|dive into|explore|take a look|unpack)\b|it'?s (worth noting|important to note|no secret)\b)

rules.title: Ending that gestures instead of concluding
rules.why: Machine-written pieces end by reaching for significance, because there is nothing left to say and the shape demands a close.
rules.fix: End on the last real thing you have to say, or on a concrete instruction.

test.pattern: \b(in conclusion|at the end of the day|the future looks bright|possibilities are endless|only time will tell|one thing is clear|exciting times (lie )?ahead)\b

rules.title: Essay transition opening a line
rules.why: Furthermore, Moreover and Additionally are connective tissue added where the ideas are not actually connected.
rules.fix: Link the ideas by reasoning, or start the sentence at its subject.

rules.title: High-frequency model vocabulary
rules.why: Words that appear far more often in generated text than in anyone speaking. One is coincidence; a cluster is a signature.
rules.fix: Use the word you would say out loud.

rules.title: Stands as, instead of is
rules.why: Models replace a plain "is" with a verb that sounds weightier and asserts less.
rules.fix: Use is, are, or has.

test.pattern: \b(stands as an?|serves as a testament|is a testament to|stands testament|serves as a reminder)\b

rules.title: Assistant pleasantries in shipped copy
rules.why: "Great question" and "I hope this helps" are addressed to a prompt, not to a reader.
rules.fix: Delete. The reader did not ask you anything.

test.pattern: \b(great question|that'?s a great question|i hope this helps|hope that helps|happy to help)\b|\b(certainly|absolutely|of course)!

rules.title: Stacked hedging
rules.why: Two or three qualifiers on one claim, which is what gets written when nobody checked whether the claim is true.
rules.fix: Check the claim, then state it. Or name the specific uncertainty instead of gesturing at doubt.

test.pattern: \b((may|might|could|can) potentially|it (may|might|could) be possible|arguably one of the|somewhat of an?)\b

rules.title: Brochure adjectives
rules.why: Travel-brochure register. It reads as advertising even when the product is good, and it survives being pasted onto any topic, which is the giveaway.
rules.fix: Replace the adjective with the fact that made you reach for it.

rules.title: Model disclaimer left in the text
rules.why: A sentence about training data or real-time access is the model talking about itself. No human writer says it, and it tells the reader nobody read the draft.
rules.fix: Delete it. If a fact may be out of date, check it or date it.

test.pattern: \b(as of my (last|latest) (update|training)|based on (my|available) training data|i (do not|don't) have (access to )?current (data|information))\b

rules.title: Inflated significance
rules.why: Telling the reader something matters, instead of showing why, is the commonest filler in generated prose. It asserts weight the sentence has not earned.
rules.fix: Replace the claim of importance with the concrete consequence: what changed, for whom, by how much.

test.pattern: \b(plays? an? (vital|crucial|pivotal|key|significant|critical) role|underscores? the (importance|need|significance)|marks? an? (significant|pivotal|major|key) (moment|milestone|shift|turning point)|setting the stage for|enduring legacy|indelible mark|reflects broader|a (key|crucial) (turning point|moment) in)\b

rules.title: Vague attribution
rules.why: "Experts say" with no expert named is a claim wearing someone else's coat. Readers discount it, and it is often invented.
rules.fix: Name the source and link it, or state the claim as your own and stand behind it, or cut it.

rules.title: Trailing -ing analysis
rules.why: A clause like ", highlighting the importance of" bolts a vague interpretation onto a sentence that already ended. It sounds analytical and says nothing.
rules.fix: End the sentence at the fact. If the interpretation is real, give it its own sentence with a specific claim.

rules.title: Stock image from generated fiction
rules.why: These are the images and names models reach for when asked to be creative. A reader who has seen generated fiction recognises them in one line.
rules.fix: Replace with a specific, observed detail that only this piece could contain. Name characters for who they are, not for how fantasy-ish the name sounds.

test.pattern: \b(a (symphony|dance|kaleidoscope|tapestry) of|the air (was |hung )?(thick|heavy|electric) with|a shiver (ran|went) down|little did (she|he|they) know|(eyes|voice) that held|let out a breath (she|he|they) (didn't|did not) know|Elara|Seraphina|Kael|Lyra Voss|Eldoria|Thornwood)\b

rules.title: Title Case heading
rules.why: Every Word Capitalised is the default of generated markdown and reads as a template. Sentence case reads as a person.
rules.fix: Use sentence case unless the publication's house style says otherwise, then record that in the allow list.

rules.title: Emoji in a heading or list lead
rules.why: Emoji used as bullets or heading decoration is a strong tell of generated posts, especially on LinkedIn.
rules.fix: Remove it. If a symbol carries meaning, use words.
